column8: 3-49. LOCATION, LOCATION, LOCATION Bella was helping her younger sister Lea, who had been absent from school, understand decimals. When Lea came to the problem 0.37 + 0.7, she got very excited. “I know, I know!” Lea shouted, “37 and 7 make 44, so the answer is 0.44!” “Well,” Bella said, “You’re right that 37 and 7 make 44, but 0.37 is not 37 and 0.7 is not 7. The value of numbers depends on where they are located.” Bella explained, “That is why you have to line up the place values, by lining up the decimal point, when you add or subtract.” What does Bella mean? What explanation can you give for lining up decimals when adding or subtracting? Write a note to Lea explaining why 0.37 + 0.7 is not 0.44. Include the correct answer and an explanation of what each number in the problem represents. (Hint: It might help to rewrite each number as a sum of fractions or draw them with hundred blocks.)
column13: A named character (Lea) makes a specific misconception-based error (0.37 + 0.7 = 0.44), and the student is tasked with explaining why it is wrong and providing the correct answer.
column15: The paragraph presents a named student's incorrect work (Lea's addition) and asks the reader to explain the mistake and provide the correct answer, matching INCORRECT_TO_CORRECT.

4-32. Isabella is the owner of the “I’ve Been Framed!” picture-framing shop. She is excited about the work you have done describing square frames in the previous lesson and now wants your help. Use your algebraic expressions from problems 4-23 and 4-24 to help Isabella with each of the following orders. Be prepared to explain how you found each answer.
a. A customer wants a frame that has 8 tiles along each side. How many tiles will Isabella need for the whole frame?
b. Isabella’s neighbor wants a frame that has 16 tiles along each side. How many tiles will she need?
c. A new customer comes into Isabella’s shop and says he wants a frame that has 25 tiles on each side. He used the expression 4(x − 1) to calculate that he needed 99 tiles. Isabella explains that he actually needs only 96 total tiles. What mistake did the customer make?
d. Isabella’s father has 32 tiles that he wants to use to frame an old photograph. He needs to know the dimensions of the frame so that he can have the photo printed at the correct size. What should Isabella tell him?
e. Isabella has a set of 40 tiles that she bought while traveling in South Africa. What is the largest frame size (on each side) that she can make with these tiles? Will she use all of her tiles?

column8: 5-73. HOW MANY TIMES? Shane is the treasurer of the performing arts club at Jefferson High. The club wrote a budget for a trip to New York City. 9-22. Luca and Kevin calculated the volume of this rectangular box. Their work is shown.

LUCA
Volume equals length times width times height.
V = l × w × h
V = 3.38 inches × 2.5 inches × 11.5 inches
V = 97.175 inches^3

KEVIN
Volume equals the area of the base times the height.
V = B × h
V = (3.38 inches × 2.5 inches) × 11.5 inches
V = 8.45 inches^2 × 11.5 inches
V = 97.175 inches^3

a. Study the two methods. How are the two methods the same? How are they different?
b. Why are some units inches, some inches^2, and some inches^3? How did Luca and Kevin know which units to write? For additional support, refer to the Methods & Meanings box following this lesson, “Measurement in Different Dimensions.”
c. Choose one method (Luca’s or Kevin’s) to calculate the volume of the rectangular prism shown. Check your answer using the other method.
column13: Luca and Kevin present two different valid approaches to finding the volume of a rectangular prism, and students are asked to examine and compare how the two methods are the same and different.

9-53. WHICH IS SWEETER?
Kay and Bill love hummingbirds. Every spring, they hang feeders around their gardens with a mixture of water and sugar that mimics the flower nectar the birds enjoy drinking. Today, they are comparing the sweetness of their recipes.
Bill thinks his recipe is sweeter. “Mine has 5 cups of sugar and yours only has 3!”
Kay thinks hers is sweeter. “But mine has a higher percentage of sugar,” she argues.
a. Help Kay and Bill calculate the percentage of sugar in each recipe.
b. Which information is most important to decide which mixture is sweeter: the amount of sugar in each recipe, or the percentage of sugar? Which recipe makes a sweeter mixture? Discuss this with your team and be prepared to explain your ideas to the class.
